abstract: Brain function depends on protein synthesis (translation), which controls neurodevelopment, synaptic plasticity, and memory formation. To understand the molecular mechanisms of translational control, the functional states of neuronal ribosomes must be determined. We visualized the translational apparatus within induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived human neurons and in human and mouse neuron-derived lysates, using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) with high-resolution 2D template matching (2DTM) and large-area imaging (DeCo-LACE). Cryo-EM maps at up to 2.6 [A] resolution reveal structural details of numerous functional states of ribosomes. Initiating 40S subunits abundantly feature initiation factor eIF1S (also known as 5MP) indicating a tight control of translation initiation. Ribosomes with elongation factors comprise ~90% of 80S particles, suggesting a high prevalence of translating ribosomes. Most elongating ribosomes sample pre-decoding states with aminoacyl-tRNA*eEF1A*GTP and a well-resolved decoding center prior to aminoacyl-tRNA acceptance. On the large ribosomal subunit, a conserved loop of uL16 stabilizes the CCA end of peptidyl-tRNA, suggesting a ribosomal protein contribution into RNA-catalyzed peptidyl transfer. The composition of peripheral ribosomal proteins, including the P-stalk proteins proposed to be substoichiometric in neurons, is homogeneous throughout ribosome states. The compositional heterogeneity of ribosomes is therefore negligible or only occurs under specific cellular conditions. Our work provides a comprehensive visualization of ribosome states within neurons and paves the way for probing translation regulation and dysregulation in neurological diseases using cryo-EM.
